cls: Opioid agonist analgesic with norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake inhibition
pharm: Centrally acting opioid analgesic (Schedule IV controlled substance)
tags: BOXED WARNING: ultra-rapid metabolism in children
BOXED WARNING: neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome
BOXED WARNING: CNS depressant / benzodiazepine interaction
quick: ER: 100 mg once daily, max 300 mg/day
Avoid; risk of fatal respiratory depression
summary: Tramadol is a centrally acting opioid agonist that also inhibits norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake, used for severe and persistent pain requiring an opioid when alternatives are inadequate. It carries boxed warnings for addiction, abuse, misuse, and life-threatening respiratory depression, and is a Schedule IV controlled substance. It also lowers the seizure threshold and can precipitate serotonin syndrome.
indications: Management of severe and persistent pain requiring an opioid analgesic that cannot be adequately treated with alternative options, including immediate-release opioids
Not indicated as an as-needed (prn) analgesic (extended-release form)

dosage.d: Initial 100 mg once daily; titrate by 100 mg every 5 days; max 300 mg/day
dosage.t: Once daily, same time each day
dosage.n: Use lowest effective dose for shortest duration; swallow whole

dosage.d: Calculate total 24-hour IR dose, initiate ER rounded down to next lower 100 mg increment
dosage.n: Then adjust per need and tolerance

dosage.d: Discontinue other opioids (except as-needed breakthrough), initiate ER 100 mg once daily, titrate
Daily dose adjustment recommended; use caution
dosage.n: Elevated plasma concentrations and prolonged half-life in the elderly

admin: Take extended-release tablets once daily at approximately the same time every day
Swallow tablets whole; do NOT crush, chew, split, or dissolve (risk of fatal overdose)
Use the lowest effective dosage for the shortest duration consistent with treatment goals
Discuss opioid overdose reversal agents (naloxone) with patient/caregiver
Taper gradually when discontinuing to avoid withdrawal
moa: Tramadol is an opioid agonist that binds mu-opioid receptors and inhibits reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin. Its analgesic effect derives from low-affinity binding of the parent compound plus higher-affinity binding of the active O-desmethyl metabolite M1 (formed via CYP2D6), which is far more potent at the mu-opioid receptor. The monoamine reuptake inhibition contributes independently to analgesia and underlies the seizure and serotonin syndrome risk. Naloxone only partially antagonizes its analgesia.

absolute: Children younger than 12 years of age
Postoperative management in children younger than 18 years following tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy
Acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or without resuscitative equipment
Known or suspected gastrointestinal obstruction, including paralytic ileus
Concurrent use of MAO inhibitors or use within the last 14 days
relative: Adolescents 12-18 years with risk factors for respiratory depression (sleep apnea, obesity, severe pulmonary or neuromuscular disease)
Increased intracranial pressure or head injury
Seizure disorder or conditions lowering seizure threshold
monitor: Respiratory depression, especially at initiation and dose increases
Signs of addiction, abuse, and misuse
Serotonin syndrome when used with serotonergic agents

preg: Use of opioid analgesics for an extended period during pregnancy may cause neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, which can be life-threatening. Data in pregnant women are insufficient to assess birth defect or miscarriage risk; animal studies showed decreased fetal weight, reduced ossification, and increased pup mortality. Advise pregnant women of potential fetal risk and ensure neonatology management is available at delivery.
lact: Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with tramadol because of the risk of serious adverse reactions in the breastfed infant, including excess sedation and life-threatening respiratory depression, particularly in ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolizers.
renal: Use is not recommended in patients with severe renal impairment. Tramadol and its M1 metabolite undergo renal elimination, and impaired clearance increases the risk of accumulation and toxicity.
hepatic: Use is not recommended in patients with severe hepatic impairment, as metabolism of tramadol (and formation of the active M1 metabolite) is altered, increasing the risk of adverse effects.

major: MAO inhibitors (contraindicated within 14 days) - serotonin syndrome, seizures
Benzodiazepines and other CNS depressants (including alcohol) - profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death
Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, linezolid) - serotonin syndrome
Drugs that lower seizure threshold - increased seizure risk
moderate: CYP2D6 inhibitors - increase tramadol and decrease M1, altering efficacy and toxicity risk
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine) - decrease tramadol/M1 exposure, may cause withdrawal
Mixed agonist/antagonist or partial agonist opioids - may reduce effect and precipitate withdrawal
minor: Warfarin derivatives (monitor for altered anticoagulant effect)
interactions.food: Take consistently; swallow extended-release tablets whole and avoid alcohol-containing products.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - concomitant use may cause fatal respiratory depression and increases plasma drug levels.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause adrenal insufficiency; consider with abnormal cortisol or unexplained hypotension.

emergency: Respiratory depression progressing to stupor, coma, or death
Serotonin syndrome (agitation, hyperthermia, clonus, autonomic instability)

monitoring: Respiratory rate and sedation level, especially at initiation and dose increases
Signs and behaviors of addiction, abuse, and misuse (reassess regularly)
Pain control and need for continued therapy
Signs of serotonin syndrome and seizures
counsel: Swallow tablets whole; never crush, chew, or split (risk of fatal overdose)
Do not drink alcohol or take other sedatives/benzodiazepines while on tramadol
Risk of addiction even at prescribed doses; take exactly as directed
Store securely out of reach of children; accidental ingestion can be fatal
Have an opioid reversal agent (naloxone) available and know how to use it
Do not stop suddenly after prolonged use - taper to avoid withdrawal
Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you
Tell your clinician about all serotonergic medications and seizure history
pk: Store at 20-25C (68-77F); excursions 15-30C; tight, light-resistant container
pearls: Schedule IV controlled substance and habit forming - assess and reassess abuse/misuse risk
Lowers seizure threshold; risk rises with overdose, naloxone reversal, and serotonergic/seizure-threshold drugs
Serotonin syndrome can occur, especially with SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, or MAOIs
Analgesia depends on CYP2D6-mediated M1 formation; ultra-rapid metabolizers (including children) risk respiratory depression
Contraindicated in children under 12 and post-tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy under 18
Avoid combining with benzodiazepines, alcohol, or other CNS depressants
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered unless it is near the next scheduled dose; never take two doses at once or extra doses to make up. Because the extended-release form is once daily at the same time each day, contact a clinician if unsure.
overdose: Overdose may cause respiratory depression, somnolence progressing to stupor or coma, skeletal muscle flaccidity, cold/clammy skin, constricted pupils (or mydriasis with hypoxia), pulmonary edema, bradycardia, QT prolongation, hypotension, and death. Establish a patent airway and assist ventilation; give an opioid reversal agent (naloxone or nalmefene), recognizing reversal may not address all symptoms and can increase seizure risk. Seizures may be controlled with barbiturates or benzodiazepines.
